questions.question: Which statement best states the idea of popular sovereignty in the United States?
questions.correctAnswer: All governing power comes from the people, who grant it through the Constitution and elections
distractors: Government power comes from the offices themselves once they are created
The oldest branch of government holds all original power
Power belongs permanently to whichever party wins an election
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty is the founding premise that authority originates with the people. The Constitution is the instrument by which the people delegate limited powers and reserve the rest.
questions.memoryHook: The people are the landlords of power - government only rents it.

img.scene: Citizens of many ages placing ballots into a ballot box outside a stone civic building at dawn, flags hanging still, no signs or lettering visible. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The people are the landlords of power - government only rents it.
img.title: POWER FROM THE PEOPLE

questions.question: What document announced the American colonies' break from Britain and listed the reasons for it?
questions.correctAnswer: The Declaration of Independence
distractors: The Articles of Confederation
The Federalist Papers
The Northwest Ordinance
questions.explanation: Adopted on July 4, 1776, the Declaration announced independence and grounded it in natural rights and grievances against the king. The Articles came later as the first governing frame.
questions.memoryHook: 1776's break-up letter: the Declaration, signed in summer heat.

img.scene: A colonial printing office with a broadside poster of pure abstract lines hanging to dry, quills and ink pots on a wooden table, window light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1776's break-up letter: the Declaration, signed in summer heat.
img.title: DECLARING INDEPENDENCE

questions.question: According to the Declaration of Independence, what is the main job of government?
questions.correctAnswer: To secure the natural rights of the people, including life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
distractors: To expand the nation's territory whenever possible
To guarantee equal wealth for every citizen
To keep the same leaders in office for stability
questions.explanation: The Declaration holds that people form governments to secure rights they already have by nature. When a government destroys those rights, the people may alter or abolish it.
questions.memoryHook: Government is a guard hired to protect rights, not the owner of them.

img.scene: A night watchman holding a lantern beside a locked gate protecting a row of small houses, calm and reassuring mood. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Government is a guard hired to protect rights, not the owner of them.
img.title: GOVERNMENT GUARDS RIGHTS

questions.question: A state passes a law that conflicts with a valid federal law. Under the Supremacy Clause, what happens?
questions.correctAnswer: The federal law stands and the conflicting state law cannot be enforced
distractors: The state law stands because states are closer to the people
Both laws apply side by side to different citizens
The conflict is settled by whichever law is older
questions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution and laws made under it the supreme law of the land. State judges are bound by federal law when a genuine conflict exists within federal power.
questions.memoryHook: Supremacy means the top rule wins - federal over state in a true clash.

img.scene: Two overlapping road signs on blank posts where the higher larger blank shield shape covers the smaller one below, desert highway at midday. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Supremacy means the top rule wins - federal over state in a true clash.
img.title: SUPREME LAW OF THE LAND

questions.question: Why did the framers divide the national government into three separate branches?
questions.correctAnswer: So that legislative, executive and judicial powers would check one another and no single branch could dominate
distractors: So the government could hire three times as many officials
So each region of the country could control one branch
So laws could be passed three times as fast
questions.explanation: Separation of powers assigns lawmaking, enforcement and judging to different hands. Combined with checks and balances, the design makes ambition counteract ambition.
questions.memoryHook: Three branches, three locks - no one branch holds every key.

img.scene: A three-legged stone table standing level on a plaza, each leg carved in a different pattern, balanced and sturdy. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Three branches, three locks - no one branch holds every key.
img.title: THREE BRANCHES, ONE BALANCE

questions.question: A president vetoes a bill, and Congress passes it again with two-thirds of both houses. What is this sequence an example of?
questions.correctAnswer: Checks and balances: the veto and the veto override working as designed
distractors: Judicial review by the executive branch
A constitutional crisis that voids the bill
Federalism, because states must approve the law
questions.explanation: The veto lets the president check Congress; the two-thirds override lets Congress check the president back. The bill becomes law without the president's signature.
questions.memoryHook: Veto, then two-thirds - the seesaw of checks and balances.

img.scene: A large balance scale with a scroll on one pan and a quill on the other, perfectly level in a marble hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Veto, then two-thirds - the seesaw of checks and balances.
img.title: CHECKS AND BALANCES

questions.question: Which idea means government may exercise only the powers granted to it, mainly those listed in the Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: Limited government
distractors: Direct democracy
Parliamentary supremacy
Nullification
questions.explanation: Limited government is the rule-of-law principle that officials hold only delegated power. Powers not granted to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people.
questions.memoryHook: Limited means the rulebook comes first - officials stay inside it.

img.scene: A stone boundary fence with a gate around a government building, the fence clearly marking where the grounds end and open fields begin. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Limited means the rulebook comes first - officials stay inside it.
img.title: LIMITED GOVERNMENT

questions.question: Delegates at the Constitutional Convention disagreed sharply over representation. The Connecticut Compromise settled the dispute by:
questions.correctAnswer: Creating a two-house Congress: representation by population in the House and equal representation in the Senate
distractors: Giving every state one vote in a single-house legislature
Letting the president choose half of each state's delegation
Counting representation by a state's land area instead of people
questions.explanation: Large states wanted proportional representation and small states wanted equality. The compromise split the difference across two chambers, and both features survive in today's Congress.
questions.memoryHook: Connecticut split the knot: people in one house, states equal in the other.

img.scene: Two long negotiating tables merging into one hall, delegates' chairs arranged in two different patterns on either side, candles and maps with abstract shapes. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Connecticut split the knot: people in one house, states equal in the other.
img.title: THE GREAT COMPROMISE

questions.question: Federalists and Anti-Federalists argued over ratifying the Constitution. What concession finally answered the Anti-Federalists' strongest objection?
questions.correctAnswer: A promise to add a Bill of Rights protecting individual liberties against the new national government
distractors: A promise to abolish state governments within ten years
Moving the capital to a southern city
Allowing each state to print its own currency again
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists feared a distant national government without explicit rights protections. The promised first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, secured the support the Constitution needed.
questions.memoryHook: No rights list, no ratification - the Bill of Rights sealed the deal.

img.scene: A writing desk with a stack of parchment pages, the top page covered in abstract script lines, a candle and a seal stamp beside it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: No rights list, no ratification - the Bill of Rights sealed the deal.
img.title: THE BILL OF RIGHTS BARGAIN

questions.question: A citizen claims her state may simply ignore a federal law it dislikes. Which constitutional answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: No - the Supremacy Clause binds states to valid federal law; disagreement is handled through courts, elections and amendments
distractors: Yes - any state may nullify a federal law by majority vote of its legislature
Yes - but only if the governor signs a nullification order
No - because states have no power to question federal actions in any forum
questions.explanation: Nullification was rejected in practice and in case law: states may challenge federal actions in court and may seek constitutional change, but they may not unilaterally void federal law.
questions.memoryHook: Disagree in court or at the ballot box - never by ignoring the law.

img.scene: A courtroom with a tall flag stand and an empty bench, a single folder resting closed on the railing, morning light through tall windows. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Disagree in court or at the ballot box - never by ignoring the law.
img.title: CHALLENGE IN COURT, NOT BY IGNORING

questions.question: How many amendments does the United States Constitution have in total today?
questions.correctAnswer: 27 amendments
distractors: 10 amendments
17 amendments
33 amendments
questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights supplied the first ten in 1791. Seventeen more have been added since, most recently the 27th in 1992, for a total of twenty-seven.
questions.memoryHook: Ten at the start, seventeen since - twenty-seven in all.

img.scene: A long marble corridor with a row of identical framed panels stretching into the distance, each frame holding abstract parchment texture only. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Ten at the start, seventeen since - twenty-seven in all.
img.title: TWENTY-SEVEN AMENDMENTS

questions.question: What is the first step in the most commonly used method of amending the U.S. Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: Congress proposes an amendment by a two-thirds vote of both the House and the Senate
distractors: The president drafts an amendment and sends it to the states
Nine states petition the Supreme Court for an amendment
A national referendum is held to draft the text
questions.explanation: Article V's main route is proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress, followed by ratification by three-fourths of the states. Every amendment so far has used congressional proposal.
questions.memoryHook: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths ratify - Article V's two big fractions.

img.scene: A wide staircase with two long parallel flights rising to a columned building, people climbing with rolled scrolls under their arms. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths ratify - Article V's two big fractions.
img.title: PROPOSE, THEN RATIFY

questions.question: Powers such as coining money and declaring war belong to which category?
questions.correctAnswer: Delegated (enumerated) powers of the national government
distractors: Reserved powers of the states
Concurrent powers shared by both levels
Implied powers of city governments
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 8 lists powers granted to Congress, including coining money and declaring war. A written list of grants is the core of the federal design.
questions.memoryHook: Coining and war sit on the federal list - Article I, Section 8.

img.scene: A mint press stamping blank coins beside a rolled declaration scroll on a heavy oak table, guarded and orderly. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Coining and war sit on the federal list - Article I, Section 8.
img.title: POWERS ON THE FEDERAL LIST

questions.question: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the United States, nor denied to the states, to:
questions.correctAnswer: The states respectively, or to the people
distractors: The president, as chief executive
The Supreme Court
The first state to claim them
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment, the last of the Bill of Rights, states the federal bargain in one line: what the Constitution does not give the national government or forbid the states stays with states or the people.
questions.memoryHook: Tenth Amendment: whatever was not handed over stays home.

img.scene: A row of state capitol domes of different shapes along a horizon, each dome lit by the same rising sun. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Tenth Amendment: whatever was not handed over stays home.
img.title: RESERVED TO THE STATES

questions.question: Running elections, issuing driver's licenses and chartering local governments are mainly examples of:
questions.correctAnswer: State responsibilities within the federal system
distractors: Exclusive powers of the federal judiciary
Duties assigned to the president's cabinet
Powers the Constitution gives to political parties
questions.explanation: States administer most day-to-day governance: elections, licensing, schools, police and local government charters. Federal law sets some rules, but administration is a state function.
questions.memoryHook: Licenses, ballots and city charters - the states run the daily list.

img.scene: A licensing office counter with a queue of people, a ballot drop box and a small city hall model on the counter, bright and orderly. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Licenses, ballots and city charters - the states run the daily list.
img.title: STATES RUN THE DAILY LIST

questions.question: Both the national government and the states can levy taxes. Taxing is therefore a:
questions.correctAnswer: Concurrent power
distractors: Reserved power
Denied power
Implied judicial power
questions.explanation: Concurrent powers are shared: taxation, borrowing, building roads and establishing courts belong to both levels at once. The Constitution denies some powers to each level instead.
questions.memoryHook: Concurrent means both cash registers are open - two levels may tax.

img.scene: Two toll booths of different designs side by side on the same road, both open, cars passing through each lane calmly. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Concurrent means both cash registers are open - two levels may tax.
img.title: SHARED POWER TO TAX

questions.question: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court upheld Congress's power to charter a national bank by relying on:
questions.correctAnswer: The Necessary and Proper Clause - Congress may choose means that are appropriate to its enumerated powers
distractors: The Tenth Amendment's reservation of banking to the states
The president's power to create agencies by proclamation
A constitutional amendment authorizing banks
questions.explanation: Chief Justice Marshall read the Necessary and Proper Clause broadly: if an end is legitimate and within the Constitution, appropriate means are constitutional. Maryland's tax on the bank also failed.
questions.memoryHook: McCulloch: pick the goal from the list, then pick sensible tools.

img.scene: A stone bank building with tall columns at the top of wide steps, a single state tax notice board standing blank beside the entrance. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: McCulloch: pick the goal from the list, then pick sensible tools.
img.title: IMPLIED POWERS UPHELD

questions.question: A state argues that because a power is not mentioned in the Constitution, Congress may never act in that area. Which response is most accurate?
questions.correctAnswer: Congress may act where a power is delegated or fairly implied, and the Necessary and Proper Clause supports means tied to those powers
distractors: The state is right - silence always means prohibition for Congress
Congress may act anywhere a president orders it to
The question is decided by whichever level acted first in history
questions.explanation: Federal power is limited, but the limits are the grants plus fair implication from them. McCulloch and later cases keep that middle position: no general police power, but real implied means.
questions.memoryHook: Limited, yes - but the granted powers carry their tools with them.

img.scene: A toolbox open beside a blueprint on a workbench, a few well-chosen tools laid out neatly, a stone wall marking the boundary behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Limited, yes - but the granted powers carry their tools with them.
img.title: GRANTS CARRY THEIR TOOLS

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches a power with the level of government the Constitution gives it to?
questions.correctAnswer: Regulating interstate commerce - Congress; establishing local governments - the states
distractors: Regulating interstate commerce - the states; coining money - the states
Coining money - Congress; conducting foreign treaties - the states
Declaring war - the states; ratifying treaties - state legislatures
questions.explanation: The Commerce Clause assigns interstate commerce to Congress, while creating local governments is a classic reserved state function. Coining money and war powers are expressly federal, and treaties are federal as well.
questions.memoryHook: Commerce and coins go federal; city halls are born at the state level.

img.scene: A freight train crossing a state border bridge at sunrise while below it a small town hall raises a flag on its green. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Commerce and coins go federal; city halls are born at the state level.
img.title: WHO HOLDS WHICH POWER

questions.question: Why is the Necessary and Proper Clause sometimes called the Elastic Clause?
questions.correctAnswer: Because it stretches Congress's reach to any appropriate means of carrying out its listed powers
distractors: Because amendments can be stretched to cover any topic
Because it lets the president stretch a veto to any bill
Because state powers expand whenever Congress is out of session
questions.explanation: The nickname captures Marshall's reading in McCulloch: the clause lets Congress adapt its tools to new circumstances while the ends must still trace back to an enumerated power.
questions.memoryHook: Elastic stretches the tools, never the list of goals.

img.scene: A measuring tape stretching across a workbench toward a fixed wall chart of abstract columns, the tape long but anchored at one end. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Elastic stretches the tools, never the list of goals.
img.title: THE ELASTIC CLAUSE

questions.question: How many voting members serve in the United States House of Representatives?
questions.correctAnswer: 435 members
distractors: 100 members
270 members
538 members
questions.explanation: The House has had 435 voting members since the apportionment acts fixed its size; seats are divided among the states by population after each census. The Senate's 100 brings Congress to 535 voting members.
questions.memoryHook: House holds 435 - census math deals the seats.

img.scene: A vast semicircular chamber filled with long curved rows of empty seats stretching wall to wall, viewed from high above. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House holds 435 - census math deals the seats.
img.title: 435 SEATS IN THE HOUSE

questions.question: Each state elects how many United States senators, regardless of its population?
questions.correctAnswer: Two senators per state
distractors: One senator per state
Senators in proportion to population
Four senators per state
questions.explanation: Equal state representation in the Senate was the small states' half of the Connecticut Compromise. With fifty states, the Senate has one hundred members.
questions.memoryHook: Two per state, big or small - that was the bargain.

img.scene: Two identical marble chairs set before each of many varied landscape panels in a gallery, pairs repeated down the hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Two per state, big or small - that was the bargain.
img.title: TWO SENATORS EACH

questions.question: How long is a single term for a member of the U.S. House of Representatives?
questions.correctAnswer: Two years
distractors: Four years
Six years
Eight years
questions.explanation: House members face the voters every two years, the shortest federal term, keeping the chamber closest to shifting public opinion. Senators serve six and presidents four.
questions.memoryHook: House terms are marathons of two years - always campaigning weather.

img.scene: A calendar with pages flipping quickly in a breeze beside a ballot box on a porch. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House terms are marathons of two years - always campaigning weather.
img.title: TWO-YEAR HOUSE TERMS

questions.question: Which chamber of Congress has the sole power to bring charges of impeachment against a federal official?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives
distractors: The Senate
The Supreme Court
The Cabinet
questions.explanation: Impeachment is a two-step process split between the chambers: the House impeaches by majority vote, and the Senate then tries the case, with two-thirds needed to convict and remove.
questions.memoryHook: The House accuses; the Senate decides. Two chambers, two jobs.

img.scene: A gavel resting beside a sealed folder on a long table in a formal chamber, two doors visible at opposite ends of the room. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The House accuses; the Senate decides. Two chambers, two jobs.
img.title: HOUSE ACCUSES, SENATE TRIES

questions.question: A bill raising revenue - a tax bill - must begin in which chamber?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives
distractors: The Senate
Either chamber, by coin flip of the majority leaders
The Treasury Department
questions.explanation: The Origination Clause of Article I requires revenue bills to start in the House, the chamber elected directly by the people. The Senate may still amend them.
questions.memoryHook: Money bills start where the people sit closest - the House.

img.scene: A tax ledger and an abacus on a desk in a chamber with many small desks, a clerk carrying the ledger toward a doorway. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Money bills start where the people sit closest - the House.
img.title: TAX BILLS START IN THE HOUSE

questions.question: The Senate's advice-and-consent role includes confirming or rejecting which of the following?
questions.correctAnswer: Presidential nominations to the cabinet and the federal courts, and treaties
distractors: State governors chosen by legislatures
Amendments already ratified by the states
Budgets passed by the House alone
questions.explanation: Article II gives the Senate a check on the president: majority consent for major appointments and two-thirds consent for treaties. No other body performs this confirming role.
questions.memoryHook: The Senate holds the confirmation stamp for judges, cabinets and treaties.

img.scene: A long confirmation hearing table with microphones and name plates left blank, flags standing behind the empty chairs. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Senate holds the confirmation stamp for judges, cabinets and treaties.
img.title: ADVICE AND CONSENT

questions.question: After each census, House seats are reapportioned among the states. What stays fixed in that process?
questions.correctAnswer: The total of 435 seats - states gaining population gain seats only as other states lose them
distractors: Each state's share, which can never change
The total, which grows by ten seats every census
The Senate's membership, which is also reapportioned
questions.explanation: Reapportionment is zero-sum under the current statutory cap of 435. Fast-growing states pick up seats that slower-growing states give up; the Senate never changes.
questions.memoryHook: Same 435 chairs - the census just moves them around the table.

img.scene: A map table where clerks move small wooden seat markers from one region to another across a large outline map with no labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Same 435 chairs - the census just moves them around the table.
img.title: SEATS MOVE, TOTAL STAYS

questions.question: A senator wishes to block a bill by threatening an unlimited debate. In modern practice, ending that filibuster generally requires:
questions.correctAnswer: Cloture - a vote of three-fifths of the Senate, 60 of 100 senators
distractors: A simple majority of 51 senators at any moment
The vice president's sole decision
Unanimous consent of all 100 senators
questions.explanation: Senate Rule XXII lets debate be cut off by cloture, which for most business takes sixty votes. The sixty-vote threshold is why narrow majorities often cannot move contested bills.
questions.memoryHook: Sixty is the magic number to end the talking.

img.scene: A marathon speaker's podium with a tall stack of blank speech pages, a clock and many seated listeners in a grand chamber. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Sixty is the magic number to end the talking.
img.title: SIXTY TO END DEBATE

questions.question: Which list gives the constitutional qualifications for serving in the U.S. Senate?
questions.correctAnswer: At least 30 years old, a U.S. citizen for at least nine years, and an inhabitant of the state represented
distractors: At least 25 years old, a citizen for seven years, and a landowner in the state
At least 35 years old, a natural-born citizen, and a resident for 14 years
No age or citizenship requirements are stated in the Constitution
questions.explanation: Article I sets Senate qualifications at thirty years, nine years of citizenship and inhabitancy in the state. The younger House standard is twenty-five and seven; thirty-five and natural-born belongs to the presidency.
questions.memoryHook: Senate: thirty, nine and home-state. Keep the three numbers in order.

img.scene: Three bronze plaques of increasing height on a wall beside a chamber door, each plaque polished and blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Senate: thirty, nine and home-state. Keep the three numbers in order.
img.title: THIRTY, NINE, HOME STATE

questions.question: Congress passes a law, the president signs it, and a citizen argues in court that it violates the First Amendment. Which branch has the final word in that dispute?
questions.correctAnswer: The judiciary - the courts may strike the law down as unconstitutional
distractors: Congress, because it wrote the law
The president, because he signed it
The citizen's state legislature
questions.explanation: Judicial review lets courts test laws against the Constitution, and the Supreme Court's reading is final unless the Constitution is amended or the Court reverses itself. Signing and passing do not settle constitutionality.
questions.memoryHook: Passing a law is not the last word - the Constitution is, read by courts.

img.scene: A courthouse scale balancing a thick law book against a single slim constitutional volume, the slim volume's side lower and weightier. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Passing a law is not the last word - the Constitution is, read by courts.
img.title: THE FINAL WORD

questions.question: How long is one term of office for the president of the United States?
questions.correctAnswer: Four years
distractors: Two years
Six years
Seven years
questions.explanation: Article II sets a four-year presidential term. The Twenty-Second Amendment later limited a president to two elected terms.
questions.memoryHook: Four years a term, two terms the cap.

img.scene: A desk calendar with four yearly pages fanned out beside a flag in an oval office setting. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Four years a term, two terms the cap.
img.title: FOUR-YEAR TERMS

questions.question: What is the minimum age the Constitution requires for the presidency?
questions.correctAnswer: 35 years old
distractors: 25 years old
30 years old
40 years old
questions.explanation: A president must be at least thirty-five, a natural-born citizen, and a resident of the United States for at least fourteen years. The age ladder runs twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five for House, Senate and president.
questions.memoryHook: Thirty-five to drive the whole country - the top rung of the ladder.

img.scene: A staircase with three broad steps rising toward a white columned house, morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Thirty-five to drive the whole country - the top rung of the ladder.
img.title: THIRTY-FIVE FOR PRESIDENT

questions.question: Who formally elects the president of the United States?
questions.correctAnswer: The Electoral College - electors chosen in each state
distractors: The House of Representatives in every election
A direct national popular vote
The governors of the fifty states
questions.explanation: Voters choose electors, and the electors' votes, cast in their state capitals, elect the president. A candidate needs a majority of the electoral votes - 270 of 538.
questions.memoryHook: Voters pick electors; electors pick the president. Two steps, not one.

img.scene: A hall of delegates at small state tables placing sealed ballots into a large brass urn, winter light through high windows. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Voters pick electors; electors pick the president. Two steps, not one.
img.title: ELECTORS MAKE IT OFFICIAL

questions.question: How many electoral votes does a candidate need to win the presidency?
questions.correctAnswer: 270 - a majority of the 538 electoral votes
distractors: 218 - a majority of the House
100 - one for each senator
A plurality is enough; no majority is required
questions.explanation: The Electoral College has 538 electors: 435 House seats plus 100 Senate seats plus three for the District of Columbia. Half of 538 is 269, so a majority is 270.
questions.memoryHook: 538 electors, so 270 wins - majority means half plus one.

img.scene: A tally board of many small unlit squares with one bright horizontal winning line drawn across the middle, no numbers visible. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 538 electors, so 270 wins - majority means half plus one.
img.title: 270 TO WIN

questions.question: If no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, who chooses the president?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives, voting by state delegation
distractors: The Senate, voting per senator
The Supreme Court
The sitting vice president
questions.explanation: The Twelfth Amendment sends a deadlocked election to the House, where each state delegation casts one vote and a majority of states decides. It has happened twice, in 1800 and 1824.
questions.memoryHook: No 270? The House votes - one vote per state.

img.scene: Representatives gathered in small state clusters around a circular chamber, each cluster conferring over a single ballot card. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: No 270? The House votes - one vote per state.
img.title: THE HOUSE BREAKS THE TIE

questions.question: Which presidential power is checked by requiring Senate consent?
questions.correctAnswer: Making treaties with foreign nations
distractors: Granting pardons for federal crimes
Delivering the State of the Union address
Commanding the armed forces day to day
questions.explanation: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate, and major appointments need a majority, so foreign commitments carry a legislative check. Pardons, addresses and command are the president's alone.
questions.memoryHook: Treaties take a partner: two-thirds of the Senate must agree.

img.scene: Two envoys shaking hands over a sealed document on a table between two flags with abstract designs, an observer gallery behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Treaties take a partner: two-thirds of the Senate must agree.
img.title: TREATIES NEED THE SENATE

questions.question: A president is unable to serve and the vice presidency is also vacant. Under the statutory line of succession, who acts as president next?
questions.correctAnswer: The Speaker of the House
distractors: The Secretary of State
The president pro tempore of the Senate
The Chief Justice
questions.explanation: The Presidential Succession Act places the Speaker first after the vice president, then the president pro tempore, then cabinet secretaries in the order their departments were created.
questions.memoryHook: After the VP: Speaker first in line. Remember the podium order.

img.scene: A row of empty official chairs arranged in a strict line down a corridor, the first chair draped with a flag. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: After the VP: Speaker first in line. Remember the podium order.

A unitary executive in the strict sense
Executive federalism
questions.explanation: Because each officer answers to the voters rather than to the governor, Nevada's executive branch is plural: the governor cannot fire an attorney general who disagrees. The federal model concentrates appointment power far more.

The power to rewrite any bill's wording before signing
